text:
Prospective controlled study in 60 parturients testing whether the timing of crystalloid administration matters for preventing maternal hypotension during spinal anesthesia for cesarean delivery. Because crystalloids have a short intravascular dwell time, the authors hypothesized that giving the fluid just after intrathecal injection (coload) would be more effective than giving it beforehand (preload).

Methods. Parturients were randomized to receive 15 mL/kg of crystalloid either before (preload group) or immediately after (coload group) intrathecal drug injection for spinal anesthesia. Hypotension was defined as systolic arterial pressure falling below 80% of baseline, treated with ephedrine. Blood pressure, heart rate and nausea before childbirth were assessed; neonatal outcomes used Apgar scores and umbilical blood gas analysis.

Results. The incidence of hypotension was lower with coload than with preload: 53% versus 83% (p=0.026). The systolic blood pressure drop during spinal anesthesia was smaller in the coload group (25 plus/minus 10 mmHg versus 34 plus/minus 13 mmHg, p=0.002). Total ephedrine required was lower with coload: median 7.5 mg (range 0-30) versus 15 mg (range 0-40), p=0.015. Nausea was also less frequent with coload: 27% versus 60% (p=0.019). Neonatal outcome measures were comparable between groups.

Conclusion. In this study, 15 mL/kg crystalloid coload was more effective than the same volume given as preload for reducing hypotension, ephedrine use and nausea during cesarean delivery under spinal anesthesia. The volumes and timing described (15 mL/kg crystalloid as coload at intrathecal injection) are the study protocol, not a universal prescription; fluid strategy should account for maternal volume status, cardiac function and local protocol, alongside vasopressor management.
title: Influence of the timing of crystalloid administration on maternal hypotension during spinal anesthesia for cesarean delivery: preload versus coload
